title: Buddhas Enlightenment
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating equanimity and mindfulness through meditation (Zazen) to access true understanding and awakening, which is not something external to oneself, but rather an inner realization available to all beings. This awakening is not a fixed state, but a continuous process of growth and transformation that can be reenacted with each sitting in meditation. By embracing this perspective, we can deepen our connection to ourselves and others, and bring forth the teachings of Buddha anew with each practice.

sentences.text: Well, today is the actual day of Buddha's enlightenment, Rohatsu, although as I thought about writing this, it's anticlimactic after that wonderful weekend retreat we had.
In the morning we walked outside in the early dark and chanted, and the morning star was right there.
Later, during the ceremony, some folks made beautiful tissue paper flowers.
We turned this into a Buddha field of flowers.
We even got lighthearted about it.
We walked around chanting and tossing flowers, and then we started tossing them at each other.
Tim tucked one behind his ear and looked rather fetching.
It was really fun, celebrating the miracle of enlightenment, Buddha's awakening.
So even though we went through much of the celebration over the weekend, I am here to give a talk on Buddha's enlightenment, or perhaps just enlightenment in general.
All I seem to have ever read or listened to in Dharma talks is teachers saying that we are all already enlightened, so what could I possibly add?
But I made a commitment, so here goes.
I used to think Norman was just joking around when he'd say, "What is there to say?"
But I think I'm beginning to understand.
There are some things that are ineffable after a while, but we need to communicate, so I'll do it.
I guess we'll start out with the story, a cultural icon story.
We all know the standard story of Buddha's path to enlightenment.
It's in the Pali Canon and comes from the Theravada tradition, and I'll just give a brief summary here.
But I'm also going to talk about several other interpretations that I found very interesting.
The story, like the Christmas story of Buddha, as you all know: Buddha was originally named Siddhartha Gautama, of the Shakya clan in India.
Some say he was a prince and his father was a great king.
Other stories say he was just from a very, very wealthy, high caste family, whichever.
His folks were very wealthy, and his father loved him so much that he tried to wall off any and all of the misery of the world from his son.
He just wanted his son to be happy and never suffer.
I wondered, as I was writing this, we know that Buddha had a stepmom, which means somewhere along the line he lost his mom.
I don't know if that was at birth or a little later.
What struck me, and of course this is just theory, but as a child psychologist, even children who are precognitive and preverbal carry a sense of loss of the mother's womb.
Now, of course, they probably didn't know it back then.
Anyway, that's just me.
I thought I'd throw that in there.
No matter what you do, you can't protect your kid from everything, but his dad sure tried.
To continue the story, another version says that after a young life of pampering in a walled palace, Siddhartha wanted to see outside the walls.

His father, who rarely could refuse his son anything, let him venture outside the palace walls with a trusted servant, Chana, who was to make sure Siddhartha saw only the beautiful and delightful things and protect him from the ugliness that was out there.
However, as we all know, it's very difficult to bend the outside world to our will, and with each little excursion, Siddhartha would catch a glance of something he'd never seen before.
A crippled person, an old and sick person, a beggar, mourners grieving deeply in a funeral procession.
So Siddhartha asked Chana to explain these things, and was very saddened and deeply perplexed at how different the world outside the palace walls was.

During one of these excursions outside the palace, he chanced to meet a monk with a shaved head and a saffron robe, a simple bowl, and Chana explained to him that the monk had renounced the pleasures of the world in order to seek spiritual truth.
It was this meeting that intrigued him and set his plans in motion to eventually leave the palace and seek the meaning of all the suffering he had seen.
Another slightly different version I learned from one of Norman's talks is this.
He said that Buddha, when he was a young man, was visited by four mystical beings.
You could almost call them angels.
One of these beings was sickness and another was old age and another was death.
The fourth being was a spiritual mendicant who smiled at Siddhartha.
Siddhartha was horrified by the first three beings.
Remember, this was the first time he'd ever seen any of this.
He saw the mendicant as perhaps a way to be, a path to follow to try and understand this horror, this mystery of pain and suffering he never knew existed before.
He was determined to find a cure.
He thought that if he worked hard enough, he would find a cure for the suffering in this world.
So he left his father's beautiful house and riches, and he left his beautiful wife and baby son, and tried many different spiritual paths and practices.

As we know, one almost killed him, as he became such an ascetic and deprived his body of food that he eventually collapsed along a road, where fortunately a young woman carrying a container of milk found him and gently gave him the milk to drink.

After coming out of that starvation state, he could think a little more clearly, and he recognized that neither riches nor complete deprivation was helping him understand the mystery of human suffering.
He was confused, but he vowed he would just sit still under a nearby Bodhi tree, and he was not going to get up until he reached some sort of understanding of why the world is the way it is.

During this time, most stories say six years, I've seen others that say seven days, he was beset by doubts, guilt at leaving his home, leaving his family, letting them down, wanting but not wanting to be comfortably enclosed away from the pain of the world that he saw.
Then Mara, the embodiment of delusion, came to visit him and showed him all the wonders of Mara's own powers and asked him, "Where is your power?
You're just sitting there.
You could go home and have all these wonderful things to distract yourself from suffering.
Where's your power?"
Buddha refused to buy into it, he refused to be distracted, so Mara unleashed terrifying bloodthirsty warrior demons upon him, and Buddha remained steadfast and unafraid.
So then Mara decided to go after Buddha's integrity, questioned his motives, accusing him of selfish interest.
Mara said, "You're just trying to escape the suffering of this realm, and if you're so beyond this realm, why don't you just leave it?
What are you doing here?"

And it was then that Buddha reached out and touched the earth, taking all creation as his witness that there is a way beyond delusion, beyond Mara, and that it wasn't in some other realm, it was here, in everything.

It was then he saw the morning star and saw all his life and past lives pass before him, and how all of it, all the mistakes, all the virtues, everything had been right and perfect and had led him to this moment, this perfect moment of understanding that all beings in this world were just as they should be.
He was awakened, and at that moment, according to Yasutani Roshi, quoting from the Kegon Sutra, Buddha spontaneously cried out:

*Wonder of wonders, intrinsically all living beings are Buddhas endowed with wisdom and virtue, but because their minds have become inverted through delusion, delusive thinking, they fail to see this.*
And he saw that everything in the world was perfect without flaw, just as it is, and that the failure to recognize this leads to all sorts of cravings and aversions and thus suffering.
Through the equanimity found in Zazen, or just sitting, letting thoughts, feelings, temptations pass through like clouds in a vast sky, there is a way to see beyond the delusions.
From there, as we know, he formulated the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path to guide all beings to this understanding.
We know he went on to teach, and his teachings were passed down through the dedication of our female and male ancestors.
Dogen tells us that each time we sit on our cushions, we reenact Buddha's awakening and bring forth once again Buddha's awakening.
This is the story we're most familiar with, but it turns out it's not the only story.
Other Buddhist sects, I have a hard time with that word, had their own interpretation of Buddha's awakening.
But this story turned out to be the predominant version in Sri Lankan Buddhism, at the time Sri Lanka was invaded by Westerners, the English.
The English got interested in the native culture and the native religion, and they thought this was Buddhism, so they translated that particular story into English.
That became the Christmas story, in a sense, or the Easter story, of Buddha.
It became the story.
However, a Buddhist scholar named John Strong discovered and translated a different version of Buddha's awakening experience, according to a now defunct sect called Mulasarvastivada.
Their story says that Buddha loved his wife so much and was so sorrowful at the thought of leaving her that the night before he left, they made love and created a child together.
Throughout the six years of Buddha's wandering, his wife, Yashodhara, I hope I'm saying that right, her name means keeper of radiance, somehow followed his every move from home.
She stayed home, but she knew what he was doing and she did it along with him.
Even when he tried a new spiritual practice, she would too, even to the point of worrying everybody about the safety of her pregnancy when she chose to starve herself along with her husband.
The story continues that Yashodhara was pregnant for six years.
That's a pretty grim thought, and I've never even been pregnant.
I just had to sit with my friends.
But she was pregnant until the moment of her husband's awakening, and at that moment she gave birth to their son, Rahula.
Interestingly, there are two translations for this name.
In the most common story, which comes from the Theravadan tradition, and as Norman once said in a talk, okay, they're a little misogynistic, they interpreted Rahula to mean chains or binding.
In other words, not terribly supportive of having kids and being connected to a family.
However, in the Mulasarvastivada version, Rahula means God of the Moon.
There's even another version, which I admit I don't quite understand.
I'm not sure where it comes from.
It's very interesting.
It says enlightenment has always been and always will be.
Buddhas are everywhere.
Buddha is in every particle, every atom of existence, always.
In every particle of existence, there is a sitting Buddha continually awakening and thus awakening all beings, whether we know it or not.
So, stories.
Forever, it seems, humans have had to have stories to explain what they experience, what they believe in, what they're afraid of, how to make sense out of this entire confusing, baffling world.
I wonder which of these stories would mean something important to each of us.
Which one of these can you take as your way of the path that would deepen your practice because of the meaning it brings to you?
Frankly, I've always had a problem with the traditional story of Buddha leaving his wife and child.

My own abandonment issues aside, it just does not seem kind or compassionate or loving, or all of the things that we're told are integral to the practice of Buddhism, to abandon your wife and child like that.

So for me, the story of the dual journey, Buddha wandering and Yashadora at home but going through the same experiences, really resonates, as it includes both the male and the female, the seeking of wisdom without abandoning love and connection.

Also, to paraphrase Norman, it incorporates leaving home with returning home: perhaps one can leave home without actually leaving, and leaving and returning can be metaphors for spiritual change, change of old habits, of fixed views, of clinging, craving, fearing the true nature of this life.
To return home can mean that we see with new eyes, open and present and accepting of this life on its own terms, no longer needing to be so grasping and invested in our ideas of how things should be.
So what is enlightenment?
Is it fixed?
I know when I first heard of Buddhism and enlightenment, I thought, oh, you had to work really, really hard and then you get there and you stay there.
You get it, you got it, you're home free.
But in all the different sutras that we've gone over the years, it seems that after his awakening, Buddha did not exist on some lofty plane.

He lived and worked and suffered with his family, his friends, his students, but he did so with equanimity, with a heart at peace with the reality of all these things that make up a life in this earthly realm, including loss and sickness and pain and death.
I believe I've actually had moments of enlightenment, and I mean moments.
Sometimes in Zazen, sometimes in reading a particular line of a poem that strikes me clear as a bell, or a story, again, that strikes me as, yes, this is truth.

Or truly listening to someone, which I have the honor to do as a therapist, to truly listen to someone and feel absolutely present with them, clear and accepting of this reality, the truth of this moment.
So I have these moments and then they're gone.

But I do trust now, over the years, I trust that it will return as I keep practicing, as I keep an awareness about me and catch myself when I am doing battle with reality, believing I can bend it to my will, rather than, as I say over and over again, taking life on its own terms.
By that, I don't mean just accepting with resignation, "Oh yeah, I've got to accept this life, it sucks."
I mean accepting with joy, in knowing that everything is just as it should be, that it's perfect.
We're all perfect.
Now that doesn't mean that reality is static.
I don't believe that things don't change, and sometimes they even need to be challenged to change.

That, I think, is where it is so important to embrace the Eightfold Path, because it's invaluable, I think, in giving us a guide as to how we can skillfully and compassionately work for change when it's needed, without cruelly denigrating or attempting to bend someone else to our will.
I want to thank you for your patience.
I thought I was going to talk longer than this, but since we have time, I'm going to tell you something interesting I also learned from Norman.
Maybe you all already know this, but I didn't.
He told me that in all the Asian languages, there is no exact character or word for the English equivalent of enlightenment.

That concept of enlightenment is a Western concept, and it's based in what historians refer to as the Age of Enlightenment that followed the Dark Ages, when the West came out of the Dark Ages of fear and superstition and began to value reason and rationality as a basis for understanding things.
When Suzuki Roshi came to the West, he knew how Westerners thought about this and how enlightenment was seen as a positive thing.
So he intentionally used that word, very skillful means.
He purposely began to use that word to explain awakening, or the true experience of emptiness, to his students.
And really, how easy has it been for any of us, at least me, to get my brain around the concept of Buddhist emptiness?
But enlightenment, of seeing things clearly, of having the veil stripped away and just seeing things exactly as they are, I can understand that.
And to not have a vested interest in maintaining them just the way they are, I can understand that too.
So I think Suzuki Roshi was very skillful in bringing this term to us, because it's something we can work with and it makes a sort of sense in the Buddhist context.
Because of my talk, my focus has been on the different interpretations of Buddhist enlightenment and the different words that have been used and continue to be used to try and understand awakening.
I'd like to close with a quote from the philosopher Wittgenstein.

I don't know a whole lot about him, but I love this quote, because I think it speaks both to the complexity words can create for us, the traps they can create for us, and the reality that we already have everything we need.
And this is the quote.
Wittgenstein says:
*Problems are solved not by giving new information, but by arranging what we have always known.
Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by the means of language.*
Thank you.
